texts: In ischaemic mitral regurgitation the annulus moves less, above all its lateral and posterior part next to the infarct, the collar frozen along its outer side: A.
The infarcted wall pulls the papillary muscles outward, the chords tether the leaflets into a tent, and the coaptation depth increases rather than decreases.
Isolated papillary muscle dysfunction, the limp pillar in the next hotel, causes little regurgitation on its own: the ventricular wall and annulus must be distorted too.
It is systolic, not diastolic, dysfunction of the inferior wall that leads to ischaemic regurgitation.
Memory hook: the collar freezes along its side, the leaves are pulled into a tent, and the lonely limp pillar is innocent.
